title: Reducing Symmetry Increase in Equivariant Neural Networks
one_liner: When a neural network respects symmetries, symmetric inputs accidentally gain extra unwanted symmetry, losing information—this paper predicts when it happens and shows how to design features to stop it.
lead: Some neural networks are built to respect symmetries: if you rotate an object, the network's internal representation rotates the same way. These networks are useful for 3D objects, molecular structures, and any data with spatial structure. But there is a hidden trap: when the input itself is already symmetric, the output becomes even more symmetric than it should be, erasing details. This paper proves exactly when this trap springs, and shows how to redesign the feature space to avoid it.

paras: A neural network that respects symmetries (called equivariant) works like this: if you rotate the input, the output rotates the same way. This is useful because it means the network never wastes time learning the same thing in different orientations—it learns once and applies everywhere. This matters for molecules (where atoms can be rotated), 3D object recognition (where viewpoint changes), and any task where rotating or flipping the input should rotate or flip the prediction.

But here is the trap: if the input itself is already symmetric (e.g., a square, which looks the same after rotation by 90 degrees), something strange happens. The output becomes even more symmetric than it should be. A square is symmetric under 4 rotations; after the network processes it, the output might be symmetric under 8 rotations, or even all rotations. Information is lost. The network has thrown away details about orientation that the input actually contained.

callout.html: The paper proves what causes symmetric inputs to gain unwanted extra symmetry, and shows how to choose features to prevent it.

paras: The paper changes which numbers go into the feature space—the components of the network's internal representation. Instead of picking them arbitrarily, the paper gives rules: choose components whose symmetry properties are known and match the input's. This is a design choice made before training starts.

hidden.h2: Orbit type: the symmetry fingerprint of a point
hidden.name: Orbit type (symmetry class of a point)
paras: An orbit type is the answer to this question: which transformations leave a point unchanged? For a square, some points are at corners (unchanged by 90-degree rotations), some are at edge midpoints (unchanged only by 180-degree rotations), and the center is unchanged by all rotations. The set of symmetries that fix a point is called its orbit type. Different points have different orbit types.

The paper measures orbit types for every point in the input data and in the chosen feature space. It then checks: are the orbit types in the output the same as in the input? If not, information was erased. The paper provides algorithms to compute which orbit types will appear in the output, and what the smallest unavoidable set is.

heat.caption: Darker means more symmetry. Highlights show which orbit types the algorithm predicts.

reads.html: The orbit type of a point is just which rotations/reflections leave it in place. A corner of a square stays put under 4 rotations; the center stays put under all of them.
An orbit type is a conjugacy class of isotropy subgroups; the paper computes the lattice of orbit types present in a representation and tests membership via fixed-point subspace dimensions.

paras: The reason symmetry increases is mathematical: when you apply an equivariant function to a symmetric input, the constraint that the output must respect the input's symmetry can force extra symmetry in the output. The input is a list of numbers with certain symmetries; the equivariant map must respect those symmetries. But the feature space (the numbers the map can produce) might not have room for all of the input's orbit types. When an orbit type is missing from the feature space, the output must belong to a larger symmetry class just to fit the mathematical constraints—it is forced, not chosen.

The paper's fix: predict which orbit types the output will be forced to have, then choose a feature space that has exactly those orbit types available. With the right choice, every input orbit type maps to an output orbit type that preserves the same symmetry information, because the feature space has exactly the room needed—nothing more (which would cause extra symmetry), nothing less (which would cause loss).

stages.s: Symmetric input (points with different orbit types)
Check: are these orbit types available in the feature space?
If no: output forced into a larger symmetry class (lose info)
Paper's fix: pre-compute missing orbits, redesign feature space
Output: same orbit types as input (no accidental erasure)

math.words: To test whether an orbit type H is present in a feature space V, check if the dimension of the fixed points of H equals the dimension of the fixed points of all subgroups containing H.
math.equation: dim(V^H) - dim(V^{H_i}) > 0 for all H_i that strictly contain H
symbols: the set of vectors in feature space V that stay unchanged under all symmetries in orbit type H
how many free numbers in that set (its dimension)
a larger orbit type that contains H

worked.title: A concrete example: testing a square
lines: Input: square (orbit type with 4-fold rotation symmetry = group C4)
Test: are points with 4-fold symmetry available in the feature space?
Compute: vectors in feature space fixed by all 4 rotations = 3 dimensions
Difference: 3 < 6, so this test passes: 4-fold orbit type IS available
Conclusion: input symmetry can be preserved in output if features are chosen this way

math.note: The algorithm checks each orbit type by comparing fixed-point space dimensions; if the dimension increases when you go to a subgroup, the orbit type is present.

bars.h2: Loss of information: naive vs. this paper

charts.title: Naive design (arbitrary features)
charts.note: Without the paper's guidance, feature choice is arbitrary and often causes accidental symmetry. This erases input details because the unplanned feature space does not have room for all the orbit types the input contains, so the output is forced into a larger symmetry class.

charts.title: With paper's orbit-type design
charts.note: The paper's algorithm predicts exactly which orbit types must be in the feature space, then chooses features to match. This preserves the input's symmetry structure because the output orbit types are no longer forced to grow beyond what the input requires.

items.b: Choosing the wrong orbit type threshold.
items.html: If you compute the minimum forced symmetry increase but then choose features with less symmetry, information will still be lost. The algorithm gives a hard lower bound: the minimum extra symmetry that any feature space must have is fixed by the input's structure. Choosing features with less symmetry cannot reduce this forced increase—the mathematics just forces the output symmetry higher regardless.
If the symmetry of the input is not correctly recognized (e.g., confusing 4-fold rotation with 8-fold), the computed orbit types will be wrong and the feature space will be poorly matched.

items.b: Using representations with too-small orbit type sets.
items.html: Some mathematical representations just do not have certain orbit types available. If the data has those orbit types but the chosen representation does not, no amount of tuning helps, because the missing orbit type means the output must be forced into a larger symmetry class just to satisfy the equivariance constraint. The only solution is to pick a different, richer representation that has the needed orbit types.
When the input symmetry is known, the paper's algorithm computes the exact set of orbit types that must be available, and you choose a representation that has them. Information is preserved.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small neural network that processes 2D shapes (squares, triangles, etc.) with known symmetries. Train it on two tasks: (1) a task where orientation matters (e.g., classifying which way the shape is rotated), and (2) a task where you do not care (e.g., just classifying shape type). Measure whether the network's internal representation preserves the orientation information. Compare two feature designs: one chosen arbitrarily, one chosen using the paper's orbit-type algorithm.
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that the paper's feature design preserves information the naive design erases. Specifically, tasks that depend on orientation (like predicting which way a shape is rotated) must have that information available in the network's representation; the paper's design keeps it, while arbitrary feature choices erase it.
